strengths: Highly rigorous and comprehensive evaluation that directly addresses real-world query mismatch through the introduction of User-Intent Queries (UIQs).
Exposes a critical methodological issue in the community with a detailed data leakage analysis between WavCaps and standard evaluation benchmarks (AudioCaps/Clotho).

Exceptionally thorough post-hoc mechanism ablations (Appendix O) that carefully dissect the model's behavior, proving that the exclusionary query performance is driven by audio-space separability rather than just a naive text-side negation capability.
Strong and complementary empirical results, showing major improvements in text-to-text retrieval (+22% relative on MECAT) and hard negative discrimination (+4.3%p HNSR@10).
Commendable open-source contribution with the release of three UIQ benchmark datasets, code, and an interactive demo.
weaknesses: Higher computational footprint and inference latency during audio encoding compared to lightweight CLAP baselines, which may limit resource-constrained or real-time on-the-fly encoding scenarios.

On standard, clean caption-style text-to-audio benchmarks (like AudioCaps), the proposed model is slightly outperformed by M2D-CLAP, indicating that the LLM backbone's strengths lie primarily in complex, non-caption queries and text-to-text matching rather than standard descriptions.

strengths: Highly rigorous and transparent data-leakage analysis documenting significant contamination between popular pretraining sets (like WavCaps) and standard benchmarks (AudioCaps, Clotho), advocating for leakage-free evaluations on MECAT.

The creation of the User-Intent Queries (UIQ) benchmark, containing over 13,000 queries validating real-world search behaviors (e.g., questions, imperatives, keyphrases, and exclusions) verified by both human and LLM annotators.

Outstanding mechanism ablations (Appendix O) that go beyond monolithic explanations to isolate why the model performs well on negation (decoupling audio-only separation from text structure via order-shuffling controls).
Strong empirical performance, demonstrating massive improvements in text-to-text retrieval (+22% relative on MECAT) and superior hard negative discrimination metrics.
weaknesses: High computational and latency footprint compared to traditional lightweight CLAP models, requiring 3B-7B parameter LLM backbones to perform text and audio encoding.
Strong architectural dependency on native audio-multimodal LLMs, which limits immediate integration with text-only LLMs without introducing separate audio encoders.

strengths: Rigorous data leakage analysis (Section 4.1 and Appendix B) revealing substantial overlap (up to 61% in Clotho) between widely-used pretraining datasets and evaluation benchmarks, which is highly valuable for future benchmarking in the audio-text retrieval community.

Exceptionally honest and thorough post-hoc mechanism ablations (Appendix O) that dissect why the model performs well on exclusionary queries, correctly attributing the gains to audio-side embedding separation rather than overclaiming a superior linguistic negation capability in the text encoder.
Introduction of the User-Intent Queries (UIQ) benchmark to move beyond unrealistic caption-style queries toward diverse real-world formulations (questions, commands, tags, paraphrases, negations).
Strong performance in text-to-text (T2T) retrieval tasks and robust cross-domain generalization on leakage-free datasets like MECAT.
weaknesses: Extremely high computational and memory footprint compared to state-of-the-art dual-encoders. Table 16 shows OEA requires up to 18.3 GB peak GPU memory and has up to 10-20x slower audio encoding latency than M2D-CLAP, limiting its practicality for real-time deployment.

Mixed performance on standard text-to-audio (T2A) retrieval benchmarks. As seen in Table 2, OEA does not consistently outperform much smaller, specialized baselines like M2D-CLAP on established datasets like AudioCaps.
The UIQ benchmark relies heavily on synthetic LLM generation (GPT-5.1), which may introduce systematic stylistic biases that do not perfectly align with organic, human-written audio search queries.

The claimed 'superior semantic understanding of complex queries' is somewhat overstated given that Appendix O reveals the text-side negation processing behaves similarly to standard CLAP encoders (collapsing under word shuffles) and the benefits are mostly an artifact of wider audio-cluster spacing.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and realistic gap in audio retrieval by shifting the evaluation paradigm from synthetic caption-style queries to diverse, real-world User-Intent Queries (UIQs).

The data leakage analysis in Section 4.1 and Appendix B is exceptionally rigorous, revealing that 61% of Clotho evaluation clips are contaminated within the commonly used WavCaps training set. Surfacing this benchmark contamination is a highly valuable contribution to the community.

The proposed OEA architecture successfully demonstrates that unified multimodal LLM backbones can be adapted for retrieval via parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), leading to superior compositional and exclusionary query understanding without explicit negation training.
The introduction of hard-negative evaluation metrics (such as HNSR and TFR) offers a much more robust and realistic way to evaluate exclusionary search patterns compared to standard Recall@k.
weaknesses: High computational and memory overhead during inference: OEA requires significantly more GPU memory (11.5 GB to 18.3 GB) and exhibits slower text/audio encoding speeds compared to lightweight, highly optimized CLAP baselines, limiting its direct applicability for massive, resource-constrained databases.

While OEA excels in text-to-text matching and exclusionary queries, its overall text-to-audio (T2A) retrieval performance is comparable to, rather than consistently better than, state-of-the-art specialized models like M2D-CLAP (e.g., on AudioCaps standard T2A).

The manuscript contains a minor distracting anomaly/typo in Section 3.2.2 and Table 8, referencing query generation via 'GPT-5.1', which does not exist in public domain releases and is likely a typo for GPT-4 or GPT-4o.

strengths: The introduction of the User-Intent Queries (UIQs) taxonomy provides a highly needed and comprehensive evaluation suite reflecting real-world search behaviors (e.g., conversational, reformulation, and exclusionary queries).

An exceptionally rigorous and valuable data leakage analysis in Appendix B, which exposes that 61.0% of Clotho and 17.7% of AudioCaps evaluation clips are leaked in the popular WavCaps training dataset. This finding is highly significant for the audio-text research community.
The formulation of novel, hard negative-based evaluation metrics (HNSR@k, TFR, and Δ-Rank) that address the blind spots of standard R@k metrics in capturing actual distractor suppression.

Strong empirical performance of the OEA models, particularly showing dominance in text-to-text (T2T) retrieval and superior hard negative discrimination, demonstrating the strong linguistic priors of LLM backbones.
Exemplary experimental design, including evaluations on a leakage-free dataset (MECAT), thorough human validation with 9 annotators across 675 ratings, and code/checkpoint release plans.
weaknesses: The model's memory footprint and latency overhead, while manageable for offline audio indexing, are substantially larger than traditional, highly compact CLAP models (e.g., OEA-Nemo3B requires 11.5 GB of peak GPU memory compared to ~0.7 GB for M2D-CLAP). This limits its immediate applicability to edge devices.

The positive UIQ generation process depends heavily on a single LLM engine (GPT-5.1), which, despite strict length and vocabulary constraints, may still pass on model-specific phrasing biases to the evaluation suite.

strengths: Rigorous Data Leakage Analysis: The paper identifies and systematically addresses a major methodological flaw in current audio retrieval benchmarks—data leakage between WavCaps pretraining and AudioCaps/Clotho test sets. Implementing blocklists and testing on MECAT represents outstanding experimental hygiene.

Comprehensive Taxonomy of User Intent Queries (UIQs): Introducing five distinct query formulations (conversational, reformulation, and exclusionary) addresses a critical gap in traditional benchmarks, which rely too heavily on simplified caption-style queries.

Methodological Contribution on Negation: The development of hard negative-based evaluation metrics (HNSR, TFR, and Δ-Rank) provides a much-needed framework for evaluating how well audio retrieval systems handle complex queries with explicit exclusions.

Thorough Experimental Validation: The authors evaluate multiple LLM backbones (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B, and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) across multiple datasets, complemented by solid human validation of the synthetic benchmarks.
weaknesses: Anomalous LLM Reference (GPT-5.1): In Section 3.2.2 and Table 8, the authors state they used 'GPT-5.1' for query generation. Since GPT-5.1 is not a commercially available or publicly existing model, this is likely a typo for GPT-4 or GPT-4o, but it raises questions about reproducibility and transparency.

Massive Parameter Overhead for Modest Gains: While Omni-Embed-Audio (OEA) outperforms baselines in text-to-text (T2T) and exclusionary query retrieval, it does not consistently outperform state-of-the-art M2D-CLAP on standard text-to-audio (T2A) retrieval (e.g., on AudioCaps). Given that OEA models have billions of parameters compared to M2D-CLAP's 89M, the massive parameter scaling yields diminishing returns.

High Computational and Latency Requirements: As shown in Table 16, OEA-Qwen7B requires 18.3 GB of GPU memory and 4.86 ms for text encoding compared to M2D-CLAP's 0.7 GB memory and 0.30 ms latency. This severely limits practical deployment on resource-constrained or edge devices.

Inconsistent Scaling Trends: Moving from 3B to 7B parameters yields marginal, flat, or sometimes negative performance changes across several benchmarks (Section J). This suggests that scaling LLM backbones does not easily resolve the core bottleneck of cross-modal contrastive alignment.
